activities.caption: pair each lens with what it names
activities.name: irLensMatch

config.prompt: The three-lens toolkit — pair each lens with what it names:

pairs.right: what actors want — power, security, wealth, ideology
what happens when choices collide — cooperation or bargaining
the rules that structure both — who may do what, with whom, and who verifies it

config.why: The method is to take one real puzzle and look at it through each lens in turn — refusing the lazy answer that a single motive 'explains' a treaty or a trade dispute.

activities.caption: find the line the framework rationale refutes
activities.name: irWhySpot

config.prompt: One line of this rationale for frameworks is wrong — click it:
lines: World politics is too big and too fast to be learned as a pile of events.
Memorise every crisis of the twentieth century and you will still be unprepared for the next one.
Learn the recurring structures — who wants what, which situations repeat — and every new crisis arrives pre-organised.
A framework is a list of every car ever built.
The chapter builds the three lenses, then the discipline's own history as a fourth lens, then runs the toolkit on war itself.
config.correction: The frameworks approach is the field's version of a mechanic's training — not a list of every car, but the small set of systems every car contains.
config.why: Frameworks trade exhaustive coverage for transferable structure — that is exactly what makes the next crisis arrive pre-organised.

activities.anchor: Read the timeline through the three lenses
activities.caption: file each milestone by the rule-work it did
activities.name: irMilestoneBuckets

config.prompt: The order's dates, read through the toolkit — file each milestone:

items.label: 1648 — sovereignty entrenched: each state supreme within its territory
1815 — the great powers rebuild a balance and manage crises together
1920 — the first general organisation for collective security
1945 — collective security rebuilt with a Security Council
1947 — twenty-three states begin reciprocal tariff-cutting under agreed rules
2015 — every state pledges, none is compelled

config.why: Institutions arrive as responses to failure — and the pattern to look for is what each one could and could not enforce.

activities.anchor: without being punished by import surges
activities.caption: choose the lens, see what it reveals — and misses
activities.name: irTariffBranch

config.root: A tariff dispute lands on your desk. Which lens carries the explanation — and what does each leave out?

start.text: Two states restrict each other's goods; each government answers to industries and voters with different stakes. Pick your first analytical move:

choices.label: Ask who wants what — which industries and voters gain from the tariff
Model the collision — what happens when the two choices meet
Ask which rules could change the game

interests.text: The tariff serves some citizens at others' expense — the 'national interest' is a coalition, not a single will. What this lens leaves out: why the dispute repeats instead of ending.

choices.label: Now model the collision of choices

interactions.text: Each country gains by protecting its own industries whatever the other does, though both would gain more from open trade — a prisoner's dilemma. What this lens leaves out: how any government could ever afford to liberalise.

choices.label: Now ask which rules change the payoff table

institutions.text: Binding commitments and dispute panels let governments open their markets without retaliation — converting the dilemma into cooperation. One dispute read through all three yields a prescription — build rules — that no single lens would generate.

config.why: Each lens earns its place by explaining something the others cannot — the policy prescription no single lens would generate is the payoff of running all three.

activities.anchor: the same puzzle can be read at the level
activities.caption: drag the divider — the shortcut and the disciplined reading
activities.name: irLevelsCompare

config.prompt: The single-actor shortcut versus interests held by someone in particular — drag the divider:

before.label: The shortcut the framework refuses
before.text: 'France did X' — an actor with no preferences of its own, hiding who actually holds them: a leader, a domestic coalition, a military.

after.label: The disciplined reading
after.text: Any puzzle read at three levels — the individual leader, the domestic coalition, the international system — each actor with interests of its own, interacting through the same logic.

config.why: Interests are held by someone in particular, and finding that someone is half the analysis.

activities.anchor: in memory of the war just ended
activities.caption: rebuild the standard textbook story in sequence
activities.name: irStandardStory

config.prompt: The standard story runs in a fixed order — rebuild it:
items: 1919 — the first chair of international politics is endowed at Aberystwyth
The interwar generation believes law and the League can abolish war
1939 — E. H. Carr's The Twenty Years' Crisis
1948 — Hans Morgenthau's Politics Among Nations replaces wishful thinking with the analysis of power
The field files all this as its 'first great debate'
config.why: That is the story the forgotten history complicates: the chronology is wrong, interwar 'idealism' was more varied than the strawman, and the field's founding institutions were creations of the Anglo-American establishment.

activities.caption: true or false — what the standard story leaves out
activities.name: irForgottenJudge

statements.s: Systematic writing about international politics begins in 1919.
statements.why: It long predates 1919 — and much of it was about empire, alongside international law, diplomacy and trade.

statements.s: Chatham House and the Council on Foreign Relations were creations of the Anglo-American establishment.
statements.why: Founded in 1920 inside the establishment producing the Pax Britannica, then the Pax Americana.

statements.s: The 'first great debate' was less a debate than a later construction.
statements.why: So argue Brian Schmidt and David Long — and interwar 'idealism' was a more varied, less naive body of work than the strawman allows.

statements.s: The Pan-African congresses and Du Bois's writings on empire and peace sat at the centre of the field's canon from the start.
statements.why: They asked whether the state system itself rested on colonial domination — and were largely excluded, only now being recovered.

activities.anchor: Take one modern puzzle and test the toolkit
activities.caption: design the regime — three levers, three consequences
activities.name: irClimateBranch

config.root: Shared atmosphere, divergent economies: each state prefers others to pay for abatement and drags its own. You are designing the regime — pick a lever:

start.text: Abatement is costly to the actor and benefits everyone. Which lever do you pull first?

choices.label: Build transparency: pledge-and-review, so claims can be checked
Wait for technologies that make abatement an interest rather than a cost

transparency.text: Paris 2015 builds exactly this — weakly, and everyone knows it. It attacks the information and commitment problems, and institutions shape outcomes only as strongly as their design and their members' interests allow.

technology.text: Then the cooperation problem dissolves into coordination — everyone races for the same cheap solution, and no one gains from defecting.

enforcement.text: There is no world enforcer to impose it — the lever exists on paper only, which is why the honest lesson keeps returning to design and interests.

config.why: The lenses do not just describe; they locate the levers — technologies dissolve the dilemma into coordination, and enforcement power would change the payoffs.
